heroHeadline: Aarhus University Maps Interferon Regulation with Genome-Wide CRISPR Screens in Monocytes; Stanford's CART Nanoparticle Platform Delivers CRISPR RNA to the Corneal Endothelium, Opening a Non-Viral Path to In Vivo Eye Editing
heroSubtitle: August 18, 2026: Researchers led by Emil Aagaard Thomsen and Jacob Giehm Mikkelsen at Aarhus University, Denmark, published genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens in human monocytic cells in Science Signaling, identifying hundreds of genes — most previously unlinked to interferon biology — that support or restrict cGAS-STING-induced type I interferon responses, with implications for tuning immune reactions to CRISPR-based gene and cell therapies. August 21, 2026: Stanford University's Paul Wender and Howard Chang published in Science Advances a demonstration that their biodegradable charge-altering releasable transporter (CART) nanoparticle platform can deliver RNA — including CRISPR/Cas9 and circular RNA — selectively to the corneal endothelium. Two anterior-chamber injections produced edited alleles in 4.0–18.8% of posterior-cornea sequences in mice, and the platform also transfected human donor corneal cells and a non-human primate eye, though disease rescue, off-target effects, and repeated-dose toxicity remain unassessed.
footerNote: Data sourced from FDA, EMA, MHRA, NIH, peer-reviewed journals (Nature, Science, NEJM, Cell), ClinicalTrials.gov, and major science outlets. Clinical data reflects published peer-reviewed results only.
